name: Wiley Dunmore
languages: Spanish (picked up in Huntsville from the men in the next cells)
equipment: Leather duster, cracked and black with age, too big for him since prison
Army revolver (Colt Single Action), 5 rounds loaded and the hammer on an empty chamber
Coach gun, sawed short, in a scabbard on the remuda horse he rides
Fuse and blasting caps, in a tobacco tin, kept well away from the dynamite
A farrier's kit: rasp, nippers, a dozen shoes and nails, a small anvil horn he carries for no good reason
Saddle and tack, bedroll, canteen, a slicker
Riding horse: a ewe-necked, ugly, tireless grey mustang called Preacher, which he will not explain
A discharge from the Texas State Penitentiary at Huntsville, dated 1872, and a letter he has never sent to a woman in Sherman
features: Hard Country (Frontier-Born origin: advantage on saves against exhaustion from heat, cold, thirst and hard travel; half the usual water one day in three)

Dirty Fighting (Outlaw: once per turn, an extra 1d6 damage of the weapon's type to a creature he hits that isn't ready: surprised, not yet acted this combat, unable to see him, prone, grappled, restrained or on a spooked horse; not part of the damage on his sheet)
Hard Riding (Outlaw: advantage on Riding checks in a chase he is fleeing; mounts or dismounts with 5 ft of movement; Dash, Disengage or Hide as a bonus action)
Powder Man (Outlaw, 2nd level: lighting a fuse is part of the throw; his thrown explosives use DC 13; he sets and fuses a charge in a minute and can cut a fuse to burn from one round to an hour)

Trade: Rustler (Outlaw, 3rd level: he can move up to 50 head at a normal pace and leave a trail that needs a DC 20 Survival check to follow, and alter a brand with a running iron at advantage; he has not done either since 1868 and is not proud that he still could)

Every Horse Comes Through (Blacksmith background: he learned the forge in Huntsville; he can tell a horse's owner, how far it has come and how hard it was ridden from its shoes, and reads a horseshoe track as easily as a signature, including a bar shoe on the near fore)

personality.traits: I tell bad jokes at bad moments. I can't sit with my back to a door. I know which way every road out of every town runs, and I check, first thing, every time. I talk to horses more kindly than to people, and they talk back better.
personality.ideals: A man gets one chance to be on the right side of a thing. I missed mine. If I get another one I'm going to take it, if it kills me, and it might.
personality.bonds: Nobody, since my mother died while I was inside. A woman in Sherman I wrote a letter to and never mailed. And, it turns out, this outfit, these vaqueros and this old woman who hired an ex-convict to wrangle her horses because she said I had honest hands.
personality.flaws: In the summer of '68 I rode with Lyman Gattis on the Red River, stealing horses, and one night in Sherman he threw a lamp through a storekeeper's window with the family asleep upstairs, and I held the horses and rode away and never told anybody. I drink when I remember it, and I remember it a lot.

appearance: A wiry, stooped, weather-beaten white man of fifty-one with a seamed face, a white stubble beard, faded blue eyes that are always looking at doors, and a blacksmith's forearms. A cracked black duster too big for him, a sweat-stained hat with a rattlesnake rattle in the band, and a limp in cold weather from a guard's rifle butt.
backstory: Wiley Dunmore was born in a dogtrot cabin on the Sulphur River in 1823, rode for a cattle outfit, stole his first horse at twenty, and spent the next twenty-five years being good at a bad trade: horse thief, rustler, and in 1869 and 1870 a stage robber on the Fort Griffin road, never killing anyone, which he points out more often than he needs to. He was caught in 1870, did four years in the state penitentiary at Huntsville, learned to be a blacksmith there, and came out in 1872 with a discharge, five dollars and nowhere to go. He has been a farrier, a hostler, a mule packer and a wrangler since, and Doña Refugio hired him at the Cibolo in April to keep her remuda because her own wrangler had gone home. He did not know who the party were hunting until the night he saw a grey horse with a bar shoe at the edge of the herd's firelight and the pale man on it, and recognized Lyman Gattis, with whom he stole horses on the Red River in 1868, and who he once watched set a house afire with a thrown lamp.

dmNotes.roleplaying: Wiley is the campaign's witness to what Gattis is. Introduce him in lb-scenario-002 as the drive's wrangler, a joker who keeps the remuda and tells tall stories at the fire; let the players like him before they learn what he was. When the Riders come (or when he sees them at a distance), he recognizes Gattis and tells the party what he saw at Sherman in 1868 (CLUE C3, F3), which matches Mother Lytle's account of the lamp at Jubilee. He becomes a companion at San Lázaro or Crow's Ford, asking to ride with the party 'because I know how that man thinks, and you don't'. He reads the bar shoe, the trail, and Gattis's habits; he knows Gattis will try fire at Palomas Bend and can say so in time to wet the jacal's thatch. He is the party's explosives man and their fastest escape.
dmNotes.voice: A Sulphur River drawl, a joke for everything, a habit of saying 'I'm only telling you' before something he very much means. Goes completely flat and quiet when he talks about Gattis.
dmNotes.motivations: Primary: to be on the right side of it this time. Secondary: to see Gattis stopped, by anyone, including himself. Tertiary: to mail the letter to Sherman, which is an apology to the storekeeper's widow, if he lives.
dmNotes.secrets: Gattis knows him and will recognize him on sight; Wiley hides in the remuda when the Riders come to the herd. If they meet face to face, Gattis will offer him money to walk away, as he did in Sherman. Wiley does not know what he will say. The GM should let the moment come and let the player who is closest to Wiley decide whether to trust him; he says no.
dmNotes.attitude: Toward the party: affectionate, self-deprecating, a little desperate to be useful. Toward Saturnino and Doña Refugio: grateful and in awe. Toward Ulysses Wardlow: wary of any badge, then respectful. Toward Reverend Burris: he will confess Sherman to him, eventually, and nobody else. Toward Gattis: terror, then something harder.
